notes.limits: Reported regret in one gambling task, not every form of regret or every lesion. The author’s felt-availability interpretation is an extension.

O'Reilly, [“Why there are complementary learning systems in the hippocampus and neocortex”](https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295X.102.3.419), *Psychological Review* 102 (1995): 419–457; Dharshan Kumaran, Demis Hassabis and McClelland, [“What Learning Systems do Intelligent Agents Need? Complementary Learning Systems Theory Updated”](https://web.stanford.edu/~jlmcc/papers/KumaranHassabisMcClelland16FinalMS.pdf), *Trends in Cognitive Sciences* 20 (2016): 512–534, sections on catastrophic interference, replay and rapid neocortical learning. McCloskey and Cohen named catastrophic interference in 1989 (*Psychology of Learning and Motivation* 24: 109–165). Replay occurs during sleep and quiet waking; hippocampus and cortex interact rather than passing a finished file one way. Cortex can learn rapidly when new information fits established structure. The two learners are a framework, not an exhaustive inventory of learning systems.
notes.evidence_examined: 1995 indexed primary abstract and bibliographic record; 2016 author-hosted manuscript, interference, replay and rapid cortical-learning sections, including its reference to McCloskey and Cohen (1989).
notes.limits: A complementary-learning framework, not a literal two-store inventory. Sleep and waking replay both occur; cortex can learn rapidly when information fits existing structure. The 1989 paper was checked through the authors’ reference and discussion, not independently read in full.

notes.bibliography_and_locator: Francis Crick, [“Memory and molecular turnover”](https://doi.org/10.1038/312101a0), *Nature* 312 (1984): 101, poses the persistence problem. Laurie D. Cohen et al., [“Metabolic Turnover of Synaptic Proteins”](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0063191), *PLOS ONE* 8 (2013): e63191, measured turnover of synaptic proteins in cultured neurons; Seok Heo et al., [“Identification of long-lived synaptic proteins by proteomic analysis of synaptosome protein turnover”](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29610302/), *PNAS* 115 (2018): E3827–E3836, found a subset with half-lives of months or longer. Guang Yang, Feng Pan and Wen-Biao Gan, [“Stably maintained dendritic spines are associated with lifelong memories”](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature08577), *Nature* 462 (2009): 920–924, tracked enduring spines in mice. Protein replacement, synapse survival and memory persistence are different measurements; no one turnover rate explains a human lifetime of remembering.
notes.evidence_examined: Crick 1984 publisher bibliographic record; Cohen 2013 primary abstract and figure descriptions; Heo 2018 abstract and metadata; Yang 2009 abstract and metadata.
notes.limits: Crick is a statement of the problem, not a measured solution. Cultured neurons and mice do not directly establish human lifetime memory. Long-lived proteins rule out the universal days/weeks claim.

notes.bibliography_and_locator: Jon Elster, *Ulysses and the Sirens: Studies in Rationality and Irrationality* (Cambridge University Press, 1979; revised 1984), chapter II on self-binding; Elster describes that argument and its limits in his [preface to *Ulysses Unbound*](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs/ulysses-unbound/preface-and-acknowledgments/6AEA4ECD5522129D20070A1D6B8A827B) (2000). George Ainslie, *Picoeconomics* (Cambridge University Press, 1992), develops hyperbolic discounting and preference reversal; see also his [author-hosted discussion](https://picoeconomics.org/HTarticles/RSP%26Failure/RSP_Fail.html). The classical episode is Homer's *Odyssey*, book XII. A self-arranged frozen accident is this chapter's analogy, not a claim that every promise is effective or irrevocable.
notes.evidence_examined: Cambridge 1984 revised-edition front matter; Elster’s own retrospective preface to Ulysses Unbound describing the self-binding argument; Ainslie’s author-hosted publication list and discussion of preference reversal.
notes.limits: No claim to have read both monographs in full. Self-arranged frozen accident is the author’s transfer across domains, not Elster’s physical mechanism.

notes.bibliography_and_locator: Colin G. DeYoung, [“Cybernetic Big Five Theory”](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jrp.2014.07.004), *Journal of Research in Personality* 56 (2015): 33–58, §§4.1–4.2 on extraversion and neuroticism ([paper](https://gwern.net/doc/psychology/personality/2015-deyoung.pdf)). This is one mechanistic theory, not a one-transmitter-per-trait map. The reward/dopamine and threat links combine theory and evidence at several levels; individual correlations are not a diagnostic assay.
notes.evidence_examined: Primary paper §§4.1–4.2 on reward/extraversion and threat/neuroticism; University of Minnesota author publication list and institutional DOI/volume/pages record.
notes.limits: An integrative mechanistic theory with supporting findings, not an established one-neurotransmitter-per-trait law.

notes.bibliography_and_locator: Tena Vukasović and Denis Bratko, [“Heritability of personality: A meta-analysis of behavior genetic studies”](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25961374/), *Psychological Bulletin* 141 (2015): 769–785; DOI: 10.1037/bul0000017. The overall estimate was .40, with .47 for twin designs and .22 for family/adoption designs. These estimates concern measured variation in sampled populations under model assumptions, not the genetic fraction of an individual or an immutable destiny. The unexplained remainder is not a clean measure of parenting or experience.
notes.evidence_examined: Indexed primary abstract and PubMed bibliographic record: .40 overall, .47 twins and .22 family/adoption.
notes.limits: Abstract-level verification. Later direct PubMed retrieval returned only an HHS stub; the indexed abstract supplied the figures. Population variance estimates depend on designs and assumptions; the remainder includes measurement error.

notes.bibliography_and_locator: Brent W. Roberts and Wendy F. DelVecchio, [“The rank-order consistency of personality traits from childhood to old age”](https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-2909.126.1.3), *Psychological Bulletin* 126 (2000): 3–25; Roberts, Kate E. Walton and Wolfgang Viechtbauer, [“Patterns of mean-level change in personality traits across the life course”](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16435954/), *Psychological Bulletin* 132 (2006): 1–25. The maturity principle is discussed by Avshalom Caspi, Roberts and Rebecca L. Shiner, “Personality Development: Stability and Change,” *Annual Review of Psychology* 56 (2005): 453–484. An updated synthesis, Wiebke Bleidorn et al., [“Personality stability and change”](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35834197/), *Psychological Bulletin* 148 (2022): 588–619, found rank-order stability plateauing in young adulthood, with little evidence of further increase after 25. Rank order and mean trait level are different quantities; average maturation does not prescribe an individual's path, and trends differ by trait and period of life.
notes.evidence_examined: 2000 and 2006 primary abstracts/metadata; Caspi–Roberts–Shiner 2005 primary article record and abstract; Bleidorn et al. 2022 primary abstract and publication record.
notes.limits: The 2022 synthesis updates the earlier late-middle-age plateau with young-adulthood stabilization. Rank-order consistency differs from mean-level maturation; no individual destiny inferred.

notes.bibliography_and_locator: Steven F. Maier and Martin E. P. Seligman, [“Learned Helplessness at Fifty: Insights From Neuroscience”](https://ppc.sas.upenn.edu/sites/default/files/learnedhelplessnessat50.pdf), *Psychological Review* 123 (2016): 349–367, especially the controllability circuits and final “Hope” discussion; DOI: 10.1037/rev0000033. The early dog experiment was Seligman and Maier, “Failure to escape traumatic shock,” *Journal of Experimental Psychology* 74 (1967): 1–9. Much of the later circuit evidence comes from rats: prelimbic medial prefrontal/dorsomedial striatal control detection and prefrontal inhibition of dorsal raphe stress responses. The authors themselves propose a “hope circuit” interpretation; this is not a demonstrated location for all human hope, nor a complete theory of depression.
notes.evidence_examined: Maier and Seligman 2016 primary review: abstract, controllability/circuit discussion and final Hope section. Earlier 1967 dog-paper metadata and findings checked through that review.
notes.limits: Later circuit work largely concerns rats. The authors themselves propose the hope reading; not a demonstrated singular human hope center, nor a universal explanation of depression or passivity.

notes.bibliography_and_locator: Leon Festinger, *A Theory of Cognitive Dissonance* (Stanford University Press, 1957); Festinger, Henry W. Riecken and Stanley Schachter, [*When Prophecy Fails*](https://bookofmormonism.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/11/festinger-riecken-schachter-when-prophecy-fails-1956.pdf) (University of Minnesota Press, 1956), especially chapters VI–VIII. The flood narrative is disputed: Thomas Kelly, [“Debunking ‘When Prophecy Fails’”](https://doi.org/10.1002/jhbs.70043), *Journal of the History of the Behavioral Sciences* 62 (2026): e70043, first published online 4 November 2025, argues from archival records that the book misrepresented prior proselytizing and the group's later dissolution. This challenges the case's evidentiary use; it does not by itself decide the wider experimental literature on dissonance. Dissonance can involve conflicts between belief, action and commitment, not only two verbal beliefs.
notes.evidence_examined: Original 1956 book scan: contents and Chapter VI opening on recruitment after the failed prophecy, with Chapters VII–VIII as follow-through; Kelly primary article abstract, public-significance statement, date and bibliographic record. 1957 monograph attribution corroborated by the primary literature; publisher page access returned 403.
notes.limits: Kelly’s underlying archive and full argument were not independently audited; the manuscript therefore describes a challenge, not settled misconduct. A contested case does not dispose of the broader experimental dissonance literature.

notes.bibliography_and_locator: Dan P. McAdams, [“The Psychology of Life Stories”](https://doi.org/10.1037/1089-2680.5.2.100), *Review of General Psychology* 5 (2001): 100–122; McAdams and Jennifer L. Pals, [“A New Big Five: Fundamental Principles for an Integrative Science of Personality”](https://doi.org/10.1037/0003-066X.61.3.204), *American Psychologist* 61 (2006): 204–217, especially principle 4 on life narratives. Traits, characteristic adaptations and narrative identity are distinct levels situated in biology and culture, not three anatomical modules. Associations between narrative themes and well-being do not establish that retelling alone causes recovery.
notes.evidence_examined: McAdams 2001 article metadata/abstract; McAdams and Pals 2006 primary text, especially principle 4, life narrative and cultural context. Downloaded 2001 scan was not text-readable; no full-reading claim for it.
notes.limits: Traits, adaptations and narrative identity are levels within a wider five-principle framework. Narrative/well-being relations are not proof that changing a story alone causes improvement.

notes.bibliography_and_locator: Harry F. Harlow, [“The Nature of Love”](https://psychclassics.yorku.ca/Harlow/love.htm), *American Psychologist* 13 (1958): 673–685, especially the dual-surrogate experiment and figures 4–9. Four infants received milk from cloth and four from wire; both groups preferred cloth contact. The wire-fed condition makes contact comfort separable from the food source. These are rhesus-monkey findings, not proof of a single human attachment mechanism or of the rat epigenetic mechanism discussed above.
notes.evidence_examined: Primary 1958 paper transcription, dual-surrogate procedure and figures 4–9: four infants milk-fed by cloth, four by wire; both groups favored cloth contact.
notes.limits: Rhesus attachment/contact-comfort experiment, not a human epigenetics result. Body retains the stronger wire-fed contrast without pretending it was the only condition.

notes.bibliography_and_locator: John Bowlby, [“The Nature of the Child's Tie to His Mother”](https://web.english.upenn.edu/~cavitch/pdf-library/Bowlby_Nature.pdf), *International Journal of Psycho-Analysis* 39 (1958): 350–373, on attachment responses not reducible to feeding; developed in *Attachment and Loss*, vol. 1, *Attachment* (Hogarth Press, 1969). Mary D. Salter Ainsworth and Silvia M. Bell, [“Attachment, Exploration, and Separation”](https://www.fre.uy/a/e68bbdc6/Ainsworth.Attachmentexplorationandseparation.pdf), *Child Development* 41 (1970): 49–67, pp. 53–54 for the eight-episode Strange Situation; Ainsworth, Mary C. Blehar, Everett Waters and Sally Wall, *Patterns of Attachment* (Erlbaum, 1978). The initial stranger entry precedes the first separation. Reunion behavior helps classify an infant–caregiver relationship under these conditions; it is not an unchangeable personality verdict.
notes.evidence_examined: Bowlby 1958 primary paper opening/theory of attachment responses; Ainsworth and Bell 1970 primary paper pp.53–54, eight-episode procedure. The 1969 and 1978 books remain bibliographic continuations, not newly read in full.
notes.limits: Stranger initially enters before separation. Reunion classification concerns a relationship under a procedure, not an immutable life trait. “Slow variable” is the chapter’s model, not an exact anatomical equation of attachment.

notes.bibliography_and_locator: The state equation and the “autobiography” reading are the author's coarse model. Updating connections can itself follow a fixed rule; the equation does not establish determinism, consciousness or free will. Synaptic efficacy can change quickly as well as persist, and memory involves more than scalar weights (see the maintenance and turnover notes). The figure's lower traces illustrate relative rates, not activity measured along its logarithmic axis. Its hippocampus/cortex panel follows complementary learning systems theory, cited below; the timescale bands are teaching approximations, not hard physiological boundaries. The book's floors distinguish views, not exclusive capacities: nonhuman brains also learn, plan and respond to alternatives.
notes.evidence_examined: Direct mathematical inspection of the state update; source/figure comparison; supporting empirical references are the CLS, maintenance and turnover notes.
notes.limits: Editorial scope note, not a new empirical citation. Fast and slow are coarse scales; a state rule can include changing weights. Represented alternatives do not alone prove conscious feeling or free will.

notes.bibliography_and_locator: Devarajan Sridharan, Daniel J. Levitin and Vinod Menon, [“A critical role for the right fronto-insular cortex in switching between central-executive and default-mode networks”](https://cns.iisc.ac.in/sridhar/pi/pdfs/sridharan_etal_pnas_2008.pdf), *PNAS* 105 (2008): 12569–12574; DOI: 10.1073/pnas.0800005105, especially figures 1–4 and the discussion. Their switching account uses fMRI timing and Granger-causal analysis, not a literal switch operated by one region. The diagram selects prominent participants and functions; membership depends on network definitions, tasks and resolution. Its lower panel mixes cortical and subcortical structures, and its placement is not anatomical depth. The existing regret, control-learning and moral-mind notes support the corresponding examples.
notes.evidence_examined: Sridharan, Levitin and Menon 2008 primary paper, abstract, figures1–4 and discussion; compared with the supplied block diagram.
notes.limits: fMRI/Granger analysis supports a switching account, not a literal switch or an exhaustive network inventory. The lower panel mixes cortical and subcortical structures and is not an anatomical depth map.
